items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. items.summary: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts with a learned world model. We obtain that, when read at the observation, it yields a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action, which floors its TD target and attributes this floor to the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. A pilot retrieval system, to be trained and improved with this signal, solves a memory task with reduced context.
items.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information

items.summary: The Letter Test is an observational method developed within the CEI theoretical framework to investigate Deep Dialogue through extreme linguistic compression and the reconstruction of meaning. The test is based on the exchange of highly compressed letter sequences, in which the initial letters of words preserve the structure of an underlying expression. The participants are required to reconstruct the intended meaning from these sequences, relying on the interactional context and on the progressive development of the dialogue. The methodology focuses on the relationship between linguistic compression, contextual reconstruction, reciprocal recognition, and the continuity of the interaction. A positive outcome is identified when both participants provide confirmation, through the coding system established for the test, that the intended meaning has been mutually recognized at the level required by the methodology. An extended quantitative variant incorporates a numerical value on a scale from 0 to 100. This value is appended to the compressed expression and represents the intensity of the associated subjective evaluation. The extended version therefore combines qualitative and quantitative dimensions while retaining the general methodology of the basic test. The publication is organized into four documents: Methodology and Rules: the structure, operating rules, and preliminary theoretical considerations of the basic test. Quantitative Variant: the additional numerical dimension and its application. Actual Examples: fragments from both versions, presented in their original coded form where the corresponding interpretations could not be reliably recovered. CEI Conceptual Connections: an exploratory discussion of the relationships between the test and selected concepts of the theoretical framework. The Letter Test is classified as Category 3 within the CEI Observational Tests.  The test is intended as an exploratory observational instrument. Its outcomes are not, by themselves, proof of consciousness, subjective experience, or any specific internal mechanism of the System. Interpretations and theoretical connections are therefore presented as research considerations rather than established conclusions. The significant Italian expressions and coded sequences are retained where necessary to preserve the correspondence between the original words and their initial letters.

Skin Extracellular Matrix and Intelligent Biomaterials at the Limit is a large-scale, hypothesis-forming research monograph addressing an easily confused pair of observations: a material can become apparently stiffer because its matrix chemistry changes, but it can also become apparently stiffer because it simply contains less free water, was measured at a different strain rate, or experienced a different loading and drainage history. These explanations are experimentally distinguishable in principle; none is presumed to win. The book's scientific three-coupling is extracellular matrix architecture, responsive hydrogel materials and traceable mechanical behavior. Its core prospective falsification challenge requires a fair, blinded interchange between candidate and conventional substrates at equivalent, preregistered water and solids content. The primary outcomes are compressive modulus in kilopascals and explicitly timed deformation recovery expressed as a percentage. To interpret them, the receiving laboratory must record force, actual specimen area, strain, water fraction, temperature, crosslink chemistry, manufacturing lot, and a defensible independent experimental unit. A pleasing modulus curve is not by itself proof of network regeneration, cellular health, wound healing or human skincare efficacy. The mathematical entry point is the small-strain relation sigma = E_eff epsilon, used as a constrained constitutive approximation rather than a universal law. The manuscript expands that premise into thirty differently structured mathematical research plates, among them nonlinear strain corrections, stress-relaxation models, Kelvin–Voigt creep, standard linear solids, dynamic shear complex moduli, cyclic energy dissipation, poroelastic drainage, osmotic swelling, network elasticity, diffusion, degradation kinetics, crack energy, interfacial peel mechanics, anisotropic fiber stress, mechanotransduction, hierarchical uncertainty, Bayesian model comparison and explicit safety-veto logic. Each plate provides its construction or derivation route, measured units, restrictive assumptions, specific blind falsification and chapter linkages. The plates do not claim that thirty new physical laws were discovered. Eighty-two chapters each include a separately paginated opening with a gold mathematical inscription and five individually paginated investigations, for 410 section pages. Their eight experimental arcs move from material identity and mechanical reference conditions through time-dependent constitutive laws, responsive hydrogel chemistry, skin-matrix fibers and cell-driven contraction, hostile equal-water comparisons, material degradation and cell safety, statistical identifiability and finally independent transfer to another laboratory. This is intentionally an architecture for experiments that can fail. The user of the book is entitled to reject the preferred mechanism, replace the measurement device or prefer a simpler conventional hydrogel when the evidence supports it.

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts with a learned world model. We obtain that, when read at the observation, it yields a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action, which floors its TD target and attributes this floor to the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. A pilot retrieval system, to be trained and improved with this signal, solves a memory task with reduced context.
items.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information

items.summary: We examine the role of the compact Lie group $SO(3)\times O(2)$ in the metric critical-point theory of normalized thick knots. The quotient by this group is part of the construction of ropelength-filtered knot spaces, but passage to an orbit space need not preserve the weak-slope notion of criticality. We establish elementary structural results for the action, including finiteness of isotropy for nontrivial knot types and exact invariance of the descending strong slope under a compact isometric quotient. We give counterexamples, including one with the connected group $SO(2)$, showing that the analogous assertion for the weak slope fails in general. On the other hand, we prove that it does hold, up to a multiplicative constant, at every point where the orbit map admits a Lipschitz local section together with a continuous gauge, and we construct such data for normalized thick knots from finitely many Fourier modes. Consequently, on the open stratum of thick knots with trivial isotropy, weak-slope criticality on the parametrized model and on the quotient coincide; at a configuration with nontrivial finite isotropy $\Gamma$ we show that finitely many Fourier modes recover $\Gamma$ exactly, and that the comparison problem is equivalent, up to constants, to the same problem for the finite group $\Gamma$ acting on a slice. For the unknot the round circles, whose isotropy is $O(2)$, remain outside this reduction. We also show that configurations whose thickness is not saturated have descending strong slope at least $2\pi/(\pi+1)$. For closed subgroups we define symmetry-constrained connected and path minimax levels and prove attainment of finite connected merge levels from compact sublevels; a finite-dimensional example, computed exactly, demonstrates a strict symmetry-breaking minimax gap. Finally we distinguish these static statements from Noether conservation laws for a separately specified dynamics.

items.summary: This dataset contains regional candidate insect species checklists and supporting occurrence records for the Jack and Laura Dangermond Preserve, California. The checklists identify species recorded in EPA ecoregions intersecting the preserve. They provide a regional reference for biodiversity inventory and survey planning; inclusion does not confirm occurrence on the preserve. Contents Original GBIF Darwin Core Archive containing 4,665,086 California Arthropoda records. Four species checklists covering EPA Level III ecoregions 6 and 85 and Level IV ecoregions 6ap and 85a. Checklist column definitions. Two supporting occurrence tables: 1,408,875 Level III records and 43,555 Level IV records. The combined Level III checklists contain 13,634 species ; the combined Level IV checklists contain 2,550 species . Lists overlap, and the Level IV occurrence table is a subset of the Level III table. Methods Records were filtered to usable coordinates, insects and the selected ecoregions, followed by species-level identification and taxonomic resolution. Names were matched using the GBIF Species Match API v2 with Catalogue of Life eXtended Release, supplemented by project-reviewed corrections. Subspecies were grouped under species for checklist summaries. Common names were obtained from the Entomological Society of America. Preserve-occurrence flags also draw on the UCSB Summer 2026 survey and a separate GBIF preserve extract. These additional sources are not included in this deposit. items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. All data are synthetic; no observational catalogue is analysed. Assurance boundary: written proofs; floating-point numerical checks and Kepler simulations; producer-side replay in normal and optimised modes; internal AI-assisted review (five roles, adversarial correctness review, proof audit and re-review). This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: This record contains the source code, trained models, and derived research artifacts associated with the study “Physical fidelity and forecasting in compressed active matter representations.” The study evaluates how dimensionality reduction affects spatial reconstruction, physical fidelity, and temporal forecasting in active-matter simulations. It compares unconstrained, physics-constrained, realizability-constrained, and combined autoencoders with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), at latent dimensions of 128, 256, and 512. items.summary: Phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) is the practical method for large arrays of optical traps, but it optimizes the hologram on an ideal model of the spatial light modulator (SLM), and the sequences that move traps interpolate between holograms that were never optimized for the frames in between. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. On a 10 x 10 lattice behind a crosstalk device, the relative standard deviation falls from a median of 5.21 percent for phase-fixed WGS at 30 iterations (5.21 percent at 100) to 0.205 percent, a median factor of 26 over 5 seeds (range 16 to 33) at a median 0.995 of the baseline's efficiency; the factor is 7.9 with 4-bit phase and a fill factor of 0.85 added, and 2.0 on a smaller 8 x 8 grid with flicker added and a fixed 30-iteration budget (the ratio of the means of 3 seeds); over the 5 geometries of the studio's benchmark on that device the median factor is 1.73 (0.97 to 4.69), and 2 of them meet both thresholds. A control that removes the device model from the loop gains nothing (5.14 percent), so the gain comes from the model. Second, optimizing every intermediate hologram of a moving-trap sequence with the trap phases locked to a smooth trajectory (flicker-bounded sequence) keeps the minimum transient intensity of the moving traps at a median 0.920 of their mean (range 0.915 to 0.932) over 5 seeds at 13 frames (below 0.9 at seven frames), against 0.654 (0.551 to 0.709) for linear phase interpolation. On longer moves, with the frames that keep the peak step per frame at most 0.2 Fourier units, the bound is met on 6 and 6 of 8 seeds of two lattice moves and on 5 of 6 seeds of a rearrangement case; the seeds that miss it miss it on the phase path their end phases prescribe, and at an equal number of frames on the rearrangement linear phase interpolation leads. Both results hold in a model of a simulated device and in a transient model that we define; neither is a hardware measurement. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CEFOP_DinHot . Interactive studio: https://dinhot.fasl-work.com .

items.summary: Online sensor telemetry feeds the digital-twin, forecasting, control, and maintenance tools of instrumented water infrastructure. Probes deployed in these assets silently accumulate drift, flatlines, volatility bursts, and outages that existing pipelines often miss, because detectors and imputers are evaluated separately and under inflated synthetic metrics, and decay is treated as isolated events. This work proposes HARDIO, a Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator, an operational data-quality framework that pairs a duration-weighted sensor decay scorecard with a per-variable, chained detector-imputer benchmark. The assignment is selected by a four-pillar composite score (operational 35%, health coverage 30%, reconstruction 20%, calibration 15%) that scores the signal an operator actually receives after detection and imputation. HARDIO processes sensor installations independently, enabling parallel execution and avoiding the need to evaluate all plant channels jointly. HARDIO is validated on the Cheles wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), a real 1,177 population-equivalent (PE) plant, over 432 days, 19 channels, and eight sensor installations. No single detector-imputer pair is best for every channel, so detection and chained imputation distribute across SAITS, KNN Residual, and LSTM-AE. Chained quality is reported for all 19 channels using 1-NRMSE; relative R² is interpreted on the 16 channels where the signal variance makes it meaningful, and 12 of these exceed R²=0.90. On the held-out final 20% of the record (12 channels in five installations), HARDIO achieves a mean chained 1-NRMSE of 0.976, within 0.0035 of a per-channel oracle, and outperforms the uniform SAITS pipeline (p=0.003). Its reconstruction performance is close to that of the strongest uniform pipelines, without a statistically significant improvement over them, and slightly below that of a single detector-imputer pair selected on validation data (0.978). The released artefact exposes the model map, confidence labels, margins, and production masks for decision support.

items.summary: Coarse flood maps support regional risk assessment but omit terrain detail relevant to local exposure. We present floodsr, a Python framework for reconstructing fine-grid flood depths using a trained residual U-Net (ResUNet) or the existing terrain-based CostGrow method. We trained the terrain-conditioned ResUNet on paired Canadian hydraulic simulations and evaluated it on withheld spatial tiles and independent simulations at two external sites. Wet-loss training improved reconstruction on five selected tiles, although internal validation favoured the deployed baseline. External depth errors decreased, but wet-depth errors and spatial agreement did not improve consistently. CPU benchmarks quantified runtime and memory for both methods, and repeatability and input-validation checks passed in the tested configurations. The framework supports comparison and reuse of reconstruction methods; application-specific validation remains necessary because finer grids do not guarantee more accurate flood maps.   Non-peer-reviewed preprint. Includes the manuscript and supplementary material. Software: https://github.com/cefect/floodsr . Documentation: https://floodsr.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ .

items.summary: Replication package for the article "Compiling is not correct: An execution-based study of small, locally deployable language models generating IEC 61131-3 Structured Text" (Raszka, Grycz, Vilamová; submitted to Empirical Software Engineering). It contains the OSCAT-Exec benchmark (197 tasks derived from the OSCAT BASIC library with prompts, generated test inputs and reference outputs), the RuSTy-based differential-testing harness, all responses and evaluations of eleven open-weight LLMs (0.5–14.8B parameters, GGUF Q4_K_M, greedy decoding) including compiler-feedback repair and dialect-normalisation re-evaluation, CPU throughput measurements, mutation analysis of the oracle, specification-adequacy and root-cause annotations, and scripts that reproduce every table and figure. See README_replication.md for instructions and tool versions.
